name: Toxicity Forecasting
title: Toxicity Forecasting
answer: Toxicity forecasting in drug discovery predicts whether a candidate molecule or biologic will cause harm in humans, covering endpoints such as liver injury, heart rhythm effects, kidney damage, skin sensitization, and genotoxicity. It supports go or no go decisions before expensive animal studies and clinical trials, and it also helps with dose selection and safety monitoring. It draws on chemistry, biology, pharmacology, and computational modeling, and it is part of the broader ADMET and safety assessment workflow. In The AI Physician, it belongs to drug discovery and molecular simulation because the output is a prediction about a molecule or biological system rather than a diagnosis for a patient.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Toxicity forecasting in drug discovery predicts whether a candidate molecule or biologic will cause harm in humans, covering endpoints such as liver injury, heart rhythm effects, kidney damage, skin sensitization, and genotoxicity. It supports go or no go decisions before expensive animal studies and clinical trials, and it also helps with dose selection and safety monitoring. It draws on chemistry, biology, pharmacology, and computational modeling, and it is part of the broader ADMET and safety assessment workflow. In The AI Physician, it belongs to drug discovery and molecular simulation because the output is a prediction about a molecule or biological system rather than a diagnosis for a patient.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: Toxicity forecasting runs on curated toxicity databases, assay results, chemical structures, omics data, and sometimes electronic health records or postmarket reports. Compute ranges from laptops running classical QSAR models to GPU clusters training deep neural networks and graph neural networks. Common data sources include public toxicology databases such as Tox21 and ToxCast, chemical databases such as ChEMBL and PubChem, plus internal pharmaceutical company data. The site tracks 797 scientific models, and toxicity forecasting models are a subset of that scientific modeling landscape.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: Teams represent molecules as fingerprints, descriptors, graphs, or learned embeddings, then train statistical or machine learning models to map those representations to toxicity labels. Validation uses held out test sets, cross validation, and external validation on compounds from different chemical series, with attention to applicability domain and class imbalance. For some endpoints, mechanistic models and physiologically based pharmacokinetic models complement statistical predictions by simulating exposure at the target tissue. Results are reviewed alongside assay data and expert toxicology judgment, because a prediction is evidence, not a verdict.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Provenance matters because toxicity labels come from different assays, species, doses, and reporting standards, and mixing them without documentation can produce misleading models. Rights and risk include data licensing, patient and proprietary compound confidentiality, model bias against underrepresented chemical classes, and the possibility that a false negative could contribute to patient harm. Regulators expect model documentation, validation evidence, and human oversight, and the site's 219 compliance and regulation pages reflect that documentation burden. A toxicity forecast is usually one input to a regulated development program, not a standalone decision.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The field is moving toward multimodal models that combine chemical structure, transcriptomics, imaging, and real world evidence to predict toxicity earlier and with better mechanistic explanations. Human relevant systems such as organ on a chip and induced pluripotent stem cell assays are generating new data that may reduce reliance on animal studies and improve translation. Regulatory science is evolving toward qualification of new approach methodologies, so computational toxicity forecasts may become more accepted as part of a weight of evidence approach. The main open problems are data scarcity for rare toxicities, uncertainty quantification, and proving that a model works across diverse populations and chemical spaces.
